HelpAfs: Adaptive Flow Scale is part of Adaptive Motion Learning. From what the study measured - how far this game's picture moves from one frame to the next - it picks Flow for the game by itself: finer for slow games (75%), lighter and steadier for fast ones (35%), 50% between. Once the game is learned it replaces Game type and Flow. Turn it off to set them yourself.
WhatIsAml: Learns how your mouse, keyboard and controller move the picture in each game, so the generated frames follow your movements better. The first time, follow the short steps shown at the top of the screen.
WhatIsAfs: Picks the Flow size for each game by itself: finer for slow games, lighter for fast ones. It works with Adaptive Motion Learning.

PresetCWarning: Not recommended. Preset C lowers the image quality a lot, and the performance you gain from it is small.

SmfgAiHelp: Experimental. The frames in between are made by a neural network on your card's AI units (NVIDIA tensor cores, AMD AI accelerators, Intel XMX) - fewer pieces coming apart in fast movement and on thin things. Heavier than SMFG: about 10 ms of an RTX 3060 for each pair at x2 (SMFG: under 2), so it is for strong cards and x2 or x3. Super Video can use it on any card.
AdaptiveHelp: Frames shown a second, at an even pace (starts at the screen's refresh).
UpdateFailed: GitHub could not be reached - try again later.
TriangleMeshHelp: SMT (Super Motion Triangles): the motion read by a mesh of triangles and drawn by the graphics card directly - lighter and sharper. Off by default - turn it on to try it. With DLSS MFG or XeSS MFG it hands them the motion it reads. Off: the classic way.
WhatIsTriangleMesh: SMT - Super Motion Triangles. A mesh of triangles is laid over the picture; the motion of its corners is found by a light recursive search (3DRS) that follows the motion from one frame to the next, the mesh is cut finer where things move apart, and the graphics card draws the moved triangles directly, as it draws a game. Each generated frame costs about 40% less than SMFG's classic way, and read-outs (HUD) stay still. Off by default with every generator - turn it on to try it; off gives SMFG's classic frames. With DLSS MFG or XeSS MFG the generator still makes the frames and SMT hands it the motion of the picture. Not with SMAI: its network reads the motion. On pictures of thin repeated lines over plain areas the classic way can look better.
TriPitchHelp: Pixels between the mesh's corners. Smaller: more, finer triangles - follows small things better, but the motion found is noisier and it costs more. Larger: steadier and lighter. Default 16 px (measured best).
TriRoundsHelp: How many times each corner looks for its motion at every size (3DRS). More: finds the motion better after a fast turn, costs more for each pair of frames. Default 2.
TriFineHelp: Extra rounds that place each corner's motion between the search's texels. 0: off (lightest, least exact). Default 2.
TriFullHelp: Extra rounds on the full-size frames themselves, to the pixel. More: sharper fine detail, a little more cost. 0: off. Default 2.
TriHomeHelp: A corner whose motion does not lead back to where it started (something covered it) is not trusted, and the other frame draws that part. The number is how many pixels off still counts as trusted. Off: every corner is trusted. Default 4 px.
TriRangeHelp: How coarse the search starts for each pair. 1: short range, lightest. 2: default. 3: longest range - for very fast motion, costs more.
TriExactHelp: Rounds that place each corner's motion to a fraction of a pixel. This is what keeps fine texture sharp instead of soft and doubled. 0: off (lighter, softer). Default 2.
TriRelaxHelp: Rounds in which a corner on a plain surface (a wall, a road, the sky) takes the motion of the corners around it when that fits as well - steadier, cleaner plain areas; a thing of its own keeps its own motion. 0: off. Default 2.
UltraSmoothHelp: The smoothest motion the engine can give. Frames go out at a perfectly even pace and about one game frame of extra delay is kept in hand, so a frame that arrives late - or a short hitch of the game - is not seen. It costs that delay (about 15 ms at 60 FPS). Off: the lowest delay.
WhatIsUltraSmooth: For the smoothest picture rather than the fastest response. On: the engine keeps about one extra game frame in hand and shows every frame on a steady beat, so small stutters of the game and frames that arrive late are hidden instead of shown. The price is a little more delay between your input and the screen (about 15 ms at 60 FPS, 25 ms at 40 FPS). Off (default): the lowest delay the engine can give. Works with every generator; turn it on for slow-paced and cinematic games, leave it off for competitive ones.
EvenPacingHelp: Frames are shown at an even pace that follows the game's average frame rate, each made for its own moment - small changes in the game's frame rate no longer show in the generated frames. Turn it off to space each pair's frames over that pair alone (as before). SMFG and DLSS MFG; XeSS MFG keeps its own pacing.
WhatIsAmlGuide: The first time Adaptive Motion Learning studies a game, it shows short steps at the top of the game screen: move the camera, walk, then play freely. Leave this on to follow them - the study is done in about a minute. Turn it off to hide the steps: the game is still learned in the background from the way you play, only more slowly.
WhatIsEvenPacing: Keeps the motion smooth when the game's frame rate is not steady. On: the generated frames are shown at a regular rhythm that follows the game's average frame rate, so small ups and downs of the game's FPS are not felt. Off: each pair of real frames is filled on its own, which follows the game more tightly but shows its unevenness. Best left on, especially with a frame-rate lock. Works with SMFG and DLSS MFG (XeSS MFG keeps its own pacing).
WhatIsStretch: A game whose picture has another shape than your screen - a 4:3 game on a 16:9 screen - is shown with black bars at the sides, so nothing looks wider than it is. Turn this on to stretch the picture over the whole screen instead. If the game draws its own black bars, cut them off first with Crop input (Advanced).

HelpStart:
1. Run the game in borderless or windowed mode.
2. Choose a generator and a mode (×2 to ×6).
3. Press START MOTION, then switch to the game before the countdown ends.
4. Use the shortcut (Shift + Alt + M unless you changed it) to start and stop while you play.

If the graphics card is already at 100%, limit the game's own frame rate a little: making frames needs some room.
HelpDlss: NVIDIA's frame generation. Needs an NVIDIA RTX graphics card.
HelpXess: Intel's frame generation. It runs on many graphics cards, not all: if yours cannot run it, the app tells you.
HelpMsm: Our own generator. It works on any graphics card and is the lightest of the three. Under Advanced, “SMFG · Fast” is the lightest; “SMFG” looks for the motion more carefully.
HelpMode: Fixed: the Multiplier sets how many frames are shown for each frame of the game (×2 doubles the frame rate, ×6 shows six). Adaptive: frames are shown at an even pace of the Target (empty: the screen's refresh) whatever the game draws.
HelpGameType: Tells the engine what kind of picture to expect. “Custom” opens Flow: the share of the picture the motion is worked out at — lower is lighter, higher is finer.
HelpAml: Learns, for each game, how your mouse, keys and gamepad move the picture, how late the game follows, and where its HUD is. The first time, a short study appears at the top of the screen: follow its steps (move the camera, walk forward, then play freely for 30 seconds). Performance is a little lower while it learns and improves when it is done. Only how far the mouse and sticks move and which buttons are held is counted — never what you type. What is learned is kept per game (Settings → Cache) and helps SMFG follow fast turns and keep the HUD steady. It hears every gamepad: Xbox, DualSense, DualShock, Switch Pro and others. It also learns what your buttons do: the run button (the picture moves faster) and the aim button (the camera turns slower), used the moment you press them. Adaptive Flow Scale (part of it, can be turned off): Flow is chosen for each game from how fast its picture moves, finer for slow games and lighter and steadier for fast ones; it replaces Game type and Flow once the game is learned.
HelpUpscaling: “Sharpness only” sharpens the picture. Integer, Nearest Neighbor and Anime4K enlarge a game that runs below the screen's resolution — for pixel art, retro games and anime. SMSR 1.0 is our own AI upscaler: a small network trained on game frames makes the picture twice as large, on any card — sharper than plain scaling, and heavier: a few milliseconds every frame shown.
HelpStill: The HUD, the crosshair and on-screen text stay as sharp and steady as the game drew them.
HelpPacing: Queue target: lower gives less delay, higher gives smoother motion. Low latency keeps the delay small. Frame limit caps the frames shown; “Limit to refresh rate” never makes more frames than the screen can show.
HelpScreen: VRR: for a G-SYNC or FreeSync screen — each frame is shown the moment it is ready. Sync mode: tearing allowed, the default pacing, or VSync. HDR: turn it on when the game itself is shown in HDR.
HelpMotion: How the movement between two frames is found. Each generator has its own choices; the default is the best starting point.
HelpCapture: Capture API: how the game's picture is taken — change it only if the output is black or stutters. Game window: Borderless is best; “Scaled to screen” stretches a smaller window. Countdown: the time you have to switch to the game.
HelpGpu: Preferred GPU: the card that makes the frames. With two cards, the second can make them so the game keeps the first for itself. GPU priority “Realtime” lets the frames go first.
HelpCounter: Shows the game's own frame rate and the frame rate you see, in a corner of the picture.
HelpObs:
Screen recorders capture the game without the generated frames. To record what you actually see:
1. Install OBS Studio and the OBS Spout2 plugin (links below).
2. Here, open Advanced → Capture and turn on “Spout output (OBS)”.
3. Press START MOTION and switch to your game.
4. In OBS: Sources → + → Spout2 Capture, and choose the sender “MFG SUPER MOTION”.
5. In OBS → Settings → Video, set the FPS you want to record (60 or 120, for example).
HelpTrouble:
Black or frozen picture: use borderless mode, or try another Capture API.
Stutter or a low frame rate: choose a lower mode, “SMFG · Fast”, or limit the game's frame rate.
The engine writes what it does to %LOCALAPPDATA%\MFG SUPER MOTION\Engine\engine.log — send that file when you report a problem.
StudyDrive: Now drive a car. No car? Just stand still.
StudyNotice: Learning costs a little performance. It gets better when done.
StudyHud: Keep moving. Switch weapons or items a few times.
StudyRun: Now run: hold your run button while you move.
StudyAim: Now aim: hold your aim button and move the camera.
StudyFree: Now play as you like for 30 seconds.
WhatIsLockRefresh: Makes the motion look as even to the eye as the frame counter says. On: SMFG shows one new frame on every refresh of your screen (200 on a 200 Hz screen), each one made for the exact moment of its refresh, with VSync. The graphics card is often at 100% while the game runs, so a frame handed to the screen waits a different time for its turn every time - with VRR the screen shows it when that turn comes, and the frame times jump even though the FPS number stays steady. Locked to the refreshes, that wait no longer reaches the screen. Costs: VRR is not used for the generated frames, and about 8 ms more delay. Off: as before (the multiplier's count, VRR).
PreparingShaders: Preparing the frame generation for this PC (first time after an update only, about 15 seconds)...
MultiplierHelp: Any multiplier, such as 2.1 or 3.7: the game's own frame rate times it, never above the screen. SMFG shows the frames at an even pace; DLSS MFG and XeSS MFG can only split a pair evenly, so their pairs alternate (for 2.5: 2, 3, 2, 3 frames in between).
XessTensorHelp: XeSS MFG with Intel's model run on the tensor cores of any RTX card (through the RTX compatibility package), up to x4. RTX 20 and 30 are measured here; RTX 40 and 50 take the package's route for them, not yet run here. Other cards keep Intel's own library. The first start on a PC takes about 10 seconds.
HudAiHelp: A small network finds the game's HUD (text, numbers, minimap marks, bars, icons, crosshair, subtitles) once for each pair of real frames, on the card's AI units. Every frame in between then shows the HUD exactly as the real frame has it: not moved with the world, not doubled or smeared. Works with every generator (DLSS MFG, XeSS MFG, SMFG, SMAI). About 1 to 1.5 ms of an RTX 3060 for each pair at 1080p. It can be turned on and off while running.
HelpSmai: Our own AI generator: a small neural network (SMFG Net), trained on game recordings, makes the frames in between, through DirectML on any DirectX 12 card - cards with matrix units (NVIDIA RTX tensor cores, Intel Arc XMX, Radeon RX 7000/9000 AI accelerators) run it on them, about twice as fast. It runs once a pair of real frames, so x3 to x6 cost it about as much as x2. Windows only. Still being trained; SMFG holds the HUD steadier.
LinuxSmsrHelp: The game is told its window is half its size and draws at that size; SMSR, our AI upscaler, makes every frame whole again. Set the game to half your screen's resolution (1280x720 on 2560x1440) - or let a Vulkan game follow the window. X11 and XWayland (Proton games); not native Wayland.
ScreenLimitHelp: Never more frames than your screen shows: the same as setting the Frame limit to your screen's refresh rate (200 on a 200 Hz screen). Off: the multiplier as asked, even above the screen.
BloomHelp: The bright parts of the picture glow softly into what is around them. Added to each real frame before frames in between are made, so every generator's frames carry the same glow. Not with HDR10 (PQ).
CleanOldCache: Clean leftovers from older versions for the best performance.
